title: First Time in Seoul? A Relaxed 3-Day Itinerary (Local's Guide)

day2.note: Subway, then cable car or bus

segments.voice: Three days in Seoul. Palaces, markets, a city view at sunset, and one day that's completely yours.

If this is your first time, this plan keeps each day in one part of the city, so you spend your time looking around, not changing trains. I'll show you the route for every day, what to eat, and the small mistakes that trip up first-time visitors.
Let's start with a few things to sort out before day one.
First, check your dates. Gyeongbokgung Palace is closed on Tuesdays, and Changdeokgung Palace is closed on Mondays. If your trip falls that way, just swap day one and day three.
Second, get a transit card when you arrive. You tap it on the subway and on buses, and transfers within a short time are discounted.
Third, install Naver Map or KakaoMap. Google Maps can show you places in Korea, but its directions are limited, so a Korean map app will save you a lot of guessing.

Flying into Incheon? The AREX airport train is the simplest way into central Seoul, and airport buses and taxis are good options if you have heavy bags or arrive late. Pick whichever drops you closest to your hotel.
And where should you stay? Central Seoul works best for this plan. Around Gwanghwamun, Jongno, City Hall or Myeongdong, every stop is a short subway ride or a walk away.
Day one is all about old Seoul, and you can do the whole day on foot.

card.title: Palaces, hanok lanes and the stream

segments.voice: Start early at Gyeongbokgung Palace, the largest of Seoul's royal palaces from the Joseon dynasty. Get off at Gyeongbokgung Station on Line 3. If you arrive around opening time, the big courtyards are much quieter.

The changing of the royal guard at Gwanghwamun Gate usually happens at ten in the morning and two in the afternoon. And here's a fun one: if you wear hanbok, the traditional dress, entry to the palaces is free. There are rental shops near the station.

Give the palace about two hours. Then walk east to Anguk and the hanok lanes of Bukchon. These are real homes, so keep your voice down and stay out of doorways. Some parts of Bukchon now have visiting hours for tourists, so check the signs as you go.
When your feet need a rest, Anguk is full of cafes, and some are inside old hanok houses with wooden beams and little courtyards. Order at the counter, and it's normal to sit as long as you like.

In the afternoon, head a few minutes south to Insadong. The main street and its side alleys are full of traditional crafts, tea houses and small galleries. It's a good place for small souvenirs, like hanji paper goods.
If you want a quiet moment before dinner, step into one of Insadong's traditional tea houses. Try a herbal tea like jujube or citron, and enjoy a slower side of the city.
Finish with an evening walk along Cheonggyecheon, the stream that runs below street level from Cheonggye Plaza. It's lit up after dark, it's free, and it's an easy way to end a long first day.
Day two is for food, shopping and the best view of the city.

card.title: Markets, Myeongdong and Namsan
card.sub: Subway, then cable car or bus

segments.voice: Start at Gwangjang Market, near Jongno 5-ga Station on Line 1. It's one of Seoul's oldest markets and a great place for breakfast or an early lunch. Look for bindaetteok, a crispy mung bean pancake fried right at the stall, and mayak gimbap, little rice rolls that are hard to stop eating. Bring some cash for the stalls.

Then take the subway to Myeongdong on Line 4. It's packed with cosmetics shops and fashion stores, and from late afternoon the street food stalls open. Many shops offer tax refunds for visitors, so bring your passport when you go shopping.

From late afternoon, Myeongdong's main streets fill with food stalls. Grilled skewers, egg bread, sweet pancakes called hotteok. Most stalls take cards now, but keep a little cash just in case, and look for the price on the sign before you order.

As the sun goes down, go up Namsan to N Seoul Tower. From Myeongdong you can walk to the cable car, or take a bus up the mountain. The view is best around sunset. Cable car and observatory times change with the season, so check them that morning.
Day three is yours. Each of these options fills about half a day, so pick two.
Want more history? Visit Changdeokgung Palace and its Secret Garden. The garden can only be seen on a guided tour with its own ticket, and places are limited, so book ahead.
Into design and shopping? Go to Dongdaemun Design Plaza, and the fashion malls around Dongdaemun that stay open late.

Want to slow down like a local? Spend the afternoon in a Han River park, like Yeouido. People picnic, cycle and order fried chicken to the riverbank. Renting a bike is easy, and there's always a convenience store nearby.
Or relax properly at a jjimjilbang, a Korean bathhouse. It's one of the most local things you can do in Seoul. Just read up on the etiquette before you go.
And if you have more than three days, explore neighbourhoods like Seongsu, Hongdae or Itaewon, or take a day trip out of the city, like Suwon's Hwaseong Fortress, an easy train ride away.
Almost everything in this plan is on the subway. Tap your card in and out at the gates, and use the same card on buses.

Seoul's subway is easy for visitors. Lines have numbers and colours, station names are in English, and announcements are in English too. When you change lines, just follow the colour of the line you want.
Taxis are easy to find and fair for short trips. With the Kakao T app, you can book one without speaking any Korean.
Before you go, here are four small mistakes that catch a lot of first-time visitors.

One. Palaces on a weekend. Most sights are busiest on weekends and public holidays, so do the palaces on a weekday if you can. Two. Lunch after two o'clock. Many restaurants close for a break in the middle of the afternoon, so eat lunch early. Three. No cash at the market. Cards work almost everywhere, but carry a little cash for market stalls. And four. Trusting old opening hours. Hours and closing days change, so check each place on a map app the morning you go.

And one bonus tip. Convenience stores are your best friend in Seoul. They're on almost every corner, many are open around the clock, and you can buy water, snacks and a quick meal, and top up your transit card with cash.
A few questions people often ask. Is three days enough for Seoul? It covers the main palaces, a traditional market, a shopping street and a city view, at a comfortable pace.

card.title: Is three days enough?
card.sub: Yes, for the highlights at a relaxed pace

segments.voice: Which day should you visit Gyeongbokgung? Any day except Tuesday, when it's closed. Weekday mornings are the quietest.

Do you need to book anything? Most of this plan needs no booking at all. The one exception is the Secret Garden tour at Changdeokgung, which has limited places. Popular restaurants can also have queues at busy times.
So that's three days in Seoul. Day one, palaces, hanok lanes and the stream. Day two, a market breakfast, Myeongdong and the sunset from Namsan. Day three, whatever you love most.
